name: minizinc
why: A constraint modeling language with real solver behind it, a genuine door into combinatorial optimisation.

brief.what_it_is: MiniZinc is a high-level, solver-independent constraint modelling language for constraint satisfaction and optimisation (discrete optimisation) problems. You write a model in its own readable language, using a large library of predefined constraints. The MiniZinc compiler translates the model into FlatZinc, a solver input language, and a wide range of solvers can then run it. The homepage also describes an IDE, Python and JavaScript embedding, and in-browser use. The brew package installs the minizinc and mzn2doc executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to model constraint problems at a high level without being locked into one solver: "MiniZinc is a free and open-source constraint modeling language." The homepage stresses being able to "express and solve discrete optimisation problems" in readable, type-safe form.
brief.how_it_works: A model is compiled into FlatZinc, a lower-level solver input language, which is then handed to whichever solver you choose. Because the model and the solver are separate, the same model can run on different solver technologies. The compiler is the part in the libminizinc repository; the IDE and the solvers such as Gecode and Chuffed live in their own repositories.

commands_seen.context: From the libminizinc README: runs the n-queens model with the Gecode solver from the command line, as an alternative to the IDE's Run button.

brief.install_notes: The README recommends the bundled binary packages for Linux, Mac and Windows rather than building from source. Building the compiler needs CMake 3.4 or later and a recent C++ compiler (Clang, GCC or MSVC). Bison and Flex are optional, for lexer or parser changes. Gecode, Coin-OR CBC and proprietary solver headers (CPLEX, Gurobi, SCIP, Xpress) are optional build inputs, and CPLEX can be loaded at runtime. The IDE and solvers are not in the compiler repository, so a source build gives you the compiler alone. The brew install was not examined beyond the metadata given.
brief.standout: It is a real modelling language with a solver-independent design: one model can be sent to several different solver backends, and it has a large built-in constraint library. The homepage's example gallery and its embedding in Python, JavaScript and the browser make it approachable as a door into combinatorial optimisation.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage shows latest release 2.10.1, dated 31 August 2026 in the release notes, and the release notes describe recent work. I did not see a commit date or a GitHub release date, and the GitHub repo for MiniZinc/MiniZinc returned 404, so the libminizinc repository is the one I read.
brief.caveats: The 2.10.1 release marks the tree-sitter parser as experimental, and some syntax such as class declarations and lambdas is rejected by name. Data files use a separate, stricter grammar, and invalid data currently produces a warning, with a planned change to reject it. The brew caveats field is empty. The compiler repository excludes the IDE and solvers, so a full working setup needs the bundle or the separate repositories. Build pain is possible: the optional solver interfaces and the proprietary headers add complexity. The docs link redirected and I did not confirm the content behind it.
quotes: MiniZinc is a high-level constraint modelling language that allows you to easily express and solve discrete optimisation problems.
Run the same model using a variety of different solver technologies, without being locked into a particular solver.
Your model is then compiled into FlatZinc, a solver input language that is understood by a wide range of solvers.
